concept.name: Hammer
concept.definition: A single candlestick with a small real body near the top of the period's range, a long lower shadow (conventionally at least twice the body length), and little or no upper shadow, appearing after a downtrend. Technical analysts interpret it as a potential bullish reversal signal because sellers drove price down but buyers recovered nearly all of the loss; it is a hypothesis that requires confirmation.
concept.intuition: Sellers smashed price down during the period, but buyers hammered it back up to close near the open, showing the decline was rejected.
concept.mechanics: From OHLC data: the lower shadow (min(O, C) - L) is at least about twice the real body |C - O|, the upper shadow (H - max(O, C)) is very small, and the body sits near the high. The identical shape after an uptrend is called a hanging man; trend context, not shape, distinguishes them.
concept.formula: Hammer heuristic: (min(O, C) - L) >= 2 * |C - O| and (H - max(O, C)) <= |C - O|, after a downtrend.
concept.failure_modes: In a strong downtrend a hammer is often just a pause before further declines, so unconfirmed long entries fail frequently. Its reliability also drops on low volume or away from support levels.
concept.misconceptions: The body color is not decisive (a green close is modestly stronger, but a red hammer is still a hammer), and the shape alone is not the pattern: without a preceding downtrend it is not a hammer.
concept.example: After a month-long slide, a stock opens at 30.00, falls to 27.50, then rallies to close at 29.90. The next day a strong white candle closes above 30.50, confirming the hammer and prompting reversal-focused traders to go long with a stop below 27.50.
